title: A Thursday 18th April reflection with a cup of coffee
author: Martin Skelton
summary: Skelton turns his four states of learning (new, consolidating, treading water, drowning) into a simple practice routine for teachers and school leaders. The argument is that anyone responsible for learning needs a quick, low-stakes way of telling whether learning is actually happening in a room. He asks the reader to walk a classroom for around half an hour and make an anonymous mark on a chart each time they judge one of the four states to be present, then reflect on how sure they were. He sets out ground rules: practise alone, ignore individual students and the teacher, and look for learning rather than teaching. He illustrates with a recent visit in which he formed a hypothesis and tested it by crouching beside students and listening to their thinking. The piece is an invitation to build observational judgement through repeated, modest practice rather than through a formal evaluation tool.
points: Teachers and leaders need a fast, non-judgemental method for checking whether learning is happening, and a tally chart of the four learning states is offered as the simplest version.
Observation practice is deliberately solo, anonymous and unattached to any teacher or student, which removes the evaluative pressure that usually spoils classroom visits.
Skelton insists on at least 20 to 30 minutes in a room, because shorter pop-ins are too brief to show whether learning is occurring.
The method is to form a quick hypothesis from the room as a whole and then test it by listening to a few students at close range.
quotes: It would be helpful if teachers and school leaders and anyone else with a responsibility for learning had a quick way of knowing whether learning was happening in their classes or not. Actually, I’m going to upgrade that sentence. It is essential that teachers and school leaders have a quick way of knowing whether learning is happening or not in classrooms and learning spaces.

Simply make a dot on your chart (or a tick or a blob or whatever suits you) whenever you think you see one of the four stages of learning happening. No names, no descriptions, nothing but a single dot/tick/blob every time you think you have identified one or another kind of learning stage.
Begin your practice, your own getting better, in the spirit of new learning. Don’t expect too much too soon. Embrace any struggle you might feel.

If you are visitor to a class, DO NOT think about or look at the teacher or spend time talking with them. You don’t have time to spare. Max out the time you have with children or students. You are beginning to look for learning and NOT look for teaching.

I created a quick hypothesis of what I thought might be happening. Then I spent the rest of the lesson checking out my hypothesis with a few students, on my knees down at the student level, no more than half a metre from their brains, listening to them, watching them work, hearing their thinking, asking the occasional question (but definitely not becoming the teacher.)
I spent 30 minutes with the class. (Any less than 20 minutes is what is often called a ‘walk-through’ or a ‘pop-in’. Pleasant, but just not long enough to see if learning is happening.
